title: Retaining Wall Block Calculator
description: Count retaining wall blocks, caps, base gravel and drainage stone for any wall, with the formula and a fully worked example.

cover.alt: A curved block retaining wall being built on a gravel base with drainage stone behind it

keywords: how many retaining wall blocks do I need
retaining wall blocks per square foot
takeaways: A standard 18 x 8 in block covers 1 sq ft of wall face, so wall area in square feet is close to your block count before waste.
Count the buried bottom course in your height, or you will come up one full course short.
Plan on a 6 in compacted gravel base and 12 in of drainage stone behind the wall, not just blocks.
body:
For a 30 ft wall that is 3 ft 4 in tall in total, you need 100 wall blocks before waste, or 110 blocks with 10 percent added. This retaining wall block calculator works that out from wall length, total height and block face size, plus caps, base gravel and drainage stone.

## The formula

**Courses = total height (in) / block height (in)**

**Blocks per course = wall length (in) / block length (in), rounded up**

**Total blocks = courses x blocks per course, then add 10 percent and round up**

Total height means the full wall, including the buried bottom course. Bury at least one course so the wall does not slide or wash out. Block face size comes from the maker spec sheet. Common sizes are:

| Block face (length x height) | Face area per block | Blocks per sq ft |
| --- | --- | --- |
| 18 x 8 in | 1.00 sq ft | 1.0 |
| 16 x 6 in | 0.67 sq ft | 1.5 |
| 18 x 4 in | 0.50 sq ft | 2.0 |

The 18 x 8 in size is the Allan Block Classic and the Keystone Compac III, both at 1 block per sq ft. The 16 x 6 in size is the Keystone Legacy Stone block, at 1.5 per sq ft. For a stepped wall, work each section on its own and add them together. Our [square footage calculator](/blog/square-footage-calculator/) helps with section areas.

**Caps = wall length (in) / cap length (in), rounded up**

**Base gravel (cu ft) = length (ft) x trench width (ft) x base depth (ft)**

**Drainage stone (cu ft) = length (ft) x 1 ft wide x total height (ft)**

Divide cubic feet by 27 for cubic yards. Allan Block calls for a minimum 6 in base in a 24 in wide trench, and at least 12 in of wall rock behind the blocks.

## Worked example: a 30 ft garden wall

Say you are building a straight wall 30 ft (9.1 m) long, with 2 ft 8 in above ground, using 18 x 8 in blocks and an 18 in cap row.

Step 1, total height. One 8 in course goes below ground: 32 in above ground plus 8 in buried is 40 in.

Step 2, courses. 40 in / 8 in = 5 courses.

Step 3, blocks per course. 30 ft is 360 in. 360 in / 18 in = 20 blocks per course.

Step 4, total blocks. 5 x 20 = 100 blocks. Check by area: 30 ft x 3.33 ft is 100 sq ft, at 1 block per sq ft, so 100 blocks.

Step 5, waste. 100 x 1.10 = 110 blocks. Rounded up, buy 110.

Step 6, caps. 360 in / 18 in = 20 caps. Add 10 percent and round up, so buy 22 caps. Caps add about 4 in to finished height, per the Allan Block guide.

Step 7, base gravel. Trench 24 in wide (2 ft), base 6 in deep (0.5 ft): 30 x 2 x 0.5 = 30 cu ft. 30 / 27 = 1.11 cu yd. Rounded up, order 1.25 cu yd.

Step 8, drainage stone. Stone zone 12 in wide (1 ft) behind the full wall height: 30 x 1 x 3.33 = 100 cu ft. 100 / 27 = 3.70 cu yd. Rounded up to the next quarter yard, order 3.75 cu yd, or 4 cu yd if your supplier sells whole yards only. That also covers filling hollow block cores. Use our [gravel calculator](/blog/gravel-calculator/) to turn yards into tons.

Final order: 110 blocks, 22 caps, 1.25 cu yd of base gravel and 3.75 cu yd of drainage stone.

## How to measure your wall

Measure length along the line the wall will follow. For a curve, run a hose along the planned line and measure the hose.

Measure height at the tallest point, then check both ends. On a slope the wall steps in full courses, so price each section at its own height, not one average. Write down four numbers first: length, exposed height, block face size and cap row, yes or no.

## What changes the block count

Block size is the big one. Swap an 18 x 8 in block for a 16 x 6 in block on the same 100 sq ft wall and the count jumps from 100 to 150 blocks, because each smaller block covers 0.67 sq ft instead of 1 sq ft.

Corners and curves add cuts, and cuts eat the waste allowance. Straight walls can get by with 5 percent waste, but order 10 percent if delivery is costly.

Terraces use more blocks than one tall wall of the same total height, because each terrace needs its own buried course and cap row. Base prep for a patio next to the wall follows similar logic to our [paver calculator](/blog/paver-calculator/), and a post footing nearby uses the [concrete calculator](/blog/concrete-calculator/).

Ground conditions change the gravel, not the blocks. Soft or wet soil needs a wider, deeper trench.

## Common mistakes that leave you short

Forgetting the buried course is the most common mistake. It is a full course, the same count as every other course, and it does not show. Leave it out and you stop work on day one.

Cutting the drainage stone thin is next. Water trapped behind a wall pushes hard, and that push is a top cause of leaning walls. Keep the full 12 in zone, add a perforated drain pipe at the base for walls over 2 ft, and slope the pipe to daylight.

Last is a base course that is not level. Check each block side to side and front to back, and tap it into the compacted gravel with a rubber mallet. A block a quarter inch out on course one is an inch out by the cap row. Backfill in lifts of about 8 in, compact each lift, and do not fill the stone zone with dug out clay.

## When you need a permit or an engineer

Height is measured from the bottom of the footing or buried base to the top of the wall, not just the part you can see. Under the International Residential Code rule used in most US towns, a permit is generally not required for a wall not over 4 ft (1.2 m) in total height that supports no extra load. That extra load, called a surcharge, includes a driveway, a foundation, a pool or a steep slope above the wall.

Go past 4 ft, or add a surcharge at any height, and most towns require a permit and a design signed by a licensed engineer. Some towns set the line at 3 ft, so call your building department before you dig. Call 811 before you dig, since buried lines are often shallower than people expect.

## Frequently asked questions

### How many retaining wall blocks do I need for 100 sq ft?
With 18 x 8 in blocks, 100 blocks, or 110 with 10 percent waste. With 16 x 6 in blocks at 1.5 per sq ft, 150 blocks, or 165 with waste.

### How deep should the gravel base be under a retaining wall?
Plan on 6 in of compacted gravel or wall rock. Allan Block lists 6 in as the minimum in the base trench.

### How much drainage stone goes behind a retaining wall?
A zone at least 12 in wide, for the full wall height. For a 30 ft wall that is 3 ft 4 in tall, that is 100 cu ft, or about 3.7 cu yd.

### Do cap blocks count as a course?
No. Caps sit on top of the last course and add about 4 in of height. Count caps by length only, rounded up, plus spares for cuts.

### How tall can I build a block retaining wall without an engineer?
In most US towns, up to 4 ft in total height, including the buried course, with no driveway, structure or steep slope above it. Some towns use 3 ft.

### How many blocks are on a pallet?
It depends on the block. Keystone lists the Compac III at 45 blocks per pallet, covering 45 sq ft of face.
